passage:
Subject: The Coimbatore distribution deal

Mehak,

I'm writing instead of calling because I want to stay calm, and I want this on record.

On Friday a supplier congratulated me on "your new company's" contract with the Coimbatore distributor. I didn't know what he meant. Then I found the agreement: signed by you, three weeks ago, under a firm registered only in your name. It's the deal we built together for eight months.

I won't pretend. I've felt shock, then rage, and I haven't slept much.

Here's what I've done. I've saved copies of all our emails and invoices. I've spoken to a lawyer and to Ramesh sir, our mentor, and they'll both be present at the meeting I'm asking for this Thursday at ten.

I haven't posted anything, and I won't. I'm not interested in revenge. I'm interested in the truth and in what's fair.

Please confirm Thursday.

Chinmay

qa.a: The distributor was in Coimbatore.

qa.q: What did Chinmay feel after finding the agreement?
qa.a: Chinmay felt shock and then rage, and barely slept.

qa.q: Which of Chinmay's steps protect the business best, and why?
qa.a: Saving records, getting legal and trusted advice, and asking for a calm meeting protect the facts, while avoiding public posts keeps Chinmay from harming the case.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel receiving this email?
qa.a: Mehak may feel caught and anxious, since the calm, documented tone shows the deal is out in the open.

grounding: An email shows a young founder who discovers a partner took a deal behind their back, who secures records, seeks legal and trusted advice and asks to confront calmly instead of seeking revenge.

passage:
You asked what my first business taught me. I'm Maria, and I'll give you the short, painful version.

Parveen and I opened a bakery in Panjim with our savings. Two years of 4 a.m. starts. Then one morning the bank called about a withdrawal I hadn't made. Parveen had taken out most of our joint account to open her own café across town.

I felt like someone had punched me. I was shaking with rage. I wanted to stand outside her café and tell every customer what she'd done. I actually drafted the post.

My aunt, who runs a shop, stopped me. "First, protect yourself. Then talk." So I printed every bank statement. I changed the account passwords. I saw a lawyer about the partnership deed. Then I asked Parveen to meet at the lawyer's office, and I spoke calmly.

We settled in four months. The post stayed in my drafts. I'm glad. It would have hurt me more than her.

qa.q: Where did Maria and Parveen open their bakery?
qa.a: They opened it in Panjim.

qa.q: What did Maria feel when the bank called?
qa.a: Maria felt shocked, as if punched, and shaking with rage.

qa.q: What would you tell someone in Maria's place, based on her story?
qa.a: Secure the records and accounts first, get legal and trusted advice, and confront calmly, rather than smearing the partner publicly.

qa.q: How did Maria's aunt see the situation?
qa.a: The aunt saw that revenge would backfire and that protecting the business and records had to come first.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young founder who discovers a partner took funds behind their back, who secures records, seeks legal and trusted advice and confronts calmly instead of seeking revenge.

passage:
I'm Avni, and this is the story of the email I didn't forward.

In March, our biggest client asked for a thirty percent discount on the next order. Vandana, my co-founder, would have said no; she'd said so a dozen times. I was scared of losing them, so I said yes and didn't tell her. I told myself it would help the business.

For three weeks I felt sick every time she checked the accounts. I snapped at her over small things. When she asked why the margins looked strange, I changed the subject.

One Sunday I couldn't stand it. I went to her flat with the email printed out. "I agreed to this without you. I was wrong to hide it. I'm sorry." I didn't say it helped the business. It didn't, really; it was for my fear.

We agreed any discount above ten percent now needs both of us. She's still a bit cool with me. That's fair.

qa.a: The client asked for a thirty percent discount.

qa.q: How did Avni feel during the three weeks of hiding it?
qa.a: Avni felt sick and uneasy, snapping at Vandana and dodging her questions.

qa.q: Why did Avni avoid saying it helped the business?
qa.a: Because that excuse would not rebuild trust; owning the fear and the hiding plainly, then agreeing a new rule, was the honest repair.

qa.q: How does Vandana seem to feel after Avni's confession?
qa.a: Vandana seems hurt and still a little cool, even though they agreed a new rule together.

grounding: A first-person account shows a founder who hid a decision from a co-founder and felt uneasy, who comes clean, drops the excuse and restores their agreement.

Incubator mentor's note, Tuesday. Founders: Kavitha and Gopika, organic skincare.

Kavitha asked to see me alone today. She admitted that two months ago she hired her cousin as the company's packaging supplier without telling Gopika, and at a higher rate than the quote Gopika had found. She looked pale and kept twisting her ring. "I told myself it was quicker and family is reliable. I've felt awful every day since."

I asked what she thought Gopika would want. She said, "The truth. Before she finds the invoices."

We practised the conversation: facts first, no excuses, then a repair offer. She decided to propose that they re-tender the packaging contract together, and that any related-party deal needs both founders' written approval.

Follow-up: Kavitha told Gopika the same evening. Gopika was angry and asked for a day to think. The next morning she agreed to the re-tender. Both founders will meet me Friday.

"Did you see the newspaper piece?" Rajni asked, bright-eyed, holding up her phone. "'The young woman who put millets on every tiffin.'"

"I saw." Kashish kept stirring the test batch.

"You're quiet."

"I'm fine."

"Kashish."

Kashish put down the ladle. "Okay. I'm not fine. I built the whole supply chain. I found the farmers. And every article is about you. The investors only look at you. I've been feeling invisible. And bitter, honestly. Last week I nearly didn't send you the sales figures before your interview."

Rajni's face fell. "I didn't know. I just... answer when they call."

"I know. That's why I'm saying it to you, not to anyone else."

Rajni sat on the stool. "So what's fair?"

"Both our names in every press note. I take the investor calls on operations. And we decide together who speaks."

"Done," Rajni said. "And Kashish, thank you for telling me."

I'm Sahil, and I'll admit this: when the investor at the demo day shook Pranav's hand and walked right past mine, I wanted to trip him.

Pranav is the face of our ed-tech startup. He's good on stage. I write the code that makes the thing work. For a year, every podcast, every panel, every photo was him. I started feeling like furniture. And bitter.

The worst part was what I began doing. I stopped telling him about bugs until the last minute. Once, I let him walk into a pitch with an old slide. I told myself I was busy.

That night I saw it plainly: I was sabotaging my own company to punish my friend.

The next day I asked Pranav for coffee and said all of it, even the slide. He was quiet, then said, "You should be on stage too." We agreed: I present the product, he presents the vision, and both our names go on everything.

passage:
In Malegaon, Imran and Hemant had repaired phones side by side since they were fourteen. When they finally rented a shop together near the bus stand, nobody thought of paper. "We're brothers," Hemant said. "What paper?"

For a year it worked. Then a big order came in from a school, and they argued: who would keep the profit, who owned the new soldering machine, what if one of them wanted to leave? They had no answer. For a week they barely spoke.

Imran felt scared. Not of losing the shop. Of losing Hemant.

He asked his uncle, who had run a cloth business for thirty years. "Write it all down," his uncle said. "Paper doesn't break friendships. Guessing does."

Hemant was hurt at first. "You don't trust me?"

"I trust you completely. That's why I want nothing left to guess."

They sat with a local lawyer and wrote down roles, shares and what happens if one leaves. Hemant signed first.

qa.q: Where was their shop?
qa.a: Their shop was near the bus stand in Malegaon.

qa.q: What was Imran afraid of during the week they barely spoke?
qa.a: Imran felt scared of losing Hemant as a friend, more than losing the shop.

qa.q: Why did putting things in writing help both the friendship and the shop?
qa.a: Clear written roles, shares and exit terms removed the guessing that caused fights, protecting the friendship as well as the business.

qa.q: How did Hemant first see the idea of a written agreement?
qa.a: Hemant was hurt at first, feeling it meant Imran didn't trust him.

grounding: The passage shows two friends who ran a business on trust without contracts, and how writing down roles, shares and exit terms protected the friendship as well as the business.

passage:
Xin and Tariq met in a cooking course in Melbourne and started a dumpling stall at the Saturday market on a handshake. For eighteen months, it was perfect. Xin did the recipes, Tariq did the money and the council permits. They split everything half and half and never wrote anything down.

Then a restaurant group offered to buy them out. The buyer's lawyer asked for their partnership agreement. Xin laughed. "We don't have one. We trust each other."

The lawyer didn't laugh. "What happens if one of you wants to sell and the other doesn't?"

Xin went quiet on the tram home. She realised they had never talked about it. What if Tariq wanted to sell and she didn't? What if the friendship cracked over a question they'd never asked?

That night she said, "Tariq, I trust you with my life. I also want us to write things down, for both of us." Tariq exhaled. "Oh, thank goodness. I've been worrying too."

qa.q: What did Xin and Tariq sell at the Saturday market?
qa.a: They sold dumplings.

qa.q: What was Xin feeling on the tram home?
qa.a: Xin felt uneasy and worried, afraid the friendship might crack over a question they had never discussed.

qa.q: What wise step did Xin take, and why?
qa.a: She proposed writing down roles and exit terms while saying she trusted Tariq, because clear terms protect both the friendship and the business.

qa.q: How did Tariq feel about Xin's suggestion?
qa.a: Tariq was relieved, admitting he had been worrying too.

grounding: The passage shows a young founder who trusted her friend completely and skipped contracts, and who sees that written roles and exit terms protect the friendship as well as the business.

passage:
Advisor's note, monthly check-in. Founders: Sharmila and Ritu, handmade stationery.

The meeting started about pace: Sharmila wants to open a second outlet this year; Ritu wants to wait until the online store is profitable. Within ten minutes it was personal. Ritu said, "You always rush because you want to look important." Sharmila rolled her eyes and said, "And you hide behind spreadsheets because you're scared." Both went red and silent.

I noted the eye-roll and the "always". I told them both that contempt is the signal to stop, not to push harder.

We paused for ten minutes. Afterwards Sharmila apologised first, and admitted she was anxious they would miss their chance. Ritu said she was frightened of debt.

We agreed decision rules: any spending above a set limit needs both yeses; if they're stuck after two discussions, they bring it to me. The second outlet goes to the next meeting, with numbers from both.

qa.q: What does Sharmila want to open this year?
qa.a: She wants to open a second outlet.

qa.q: What was Sharmila anxious about underneath the argument?
qa.a: Sharmila felt anxious that they would miss their chance to grow.

qa.q: What decision rules did the founders agree, and why do they help?
qa.a: Big spending needs both yeses and a stuck decision goes to the advisor, which keeps the debate on the idea rather than on each other.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt when Sharmila rolled her eyes?
qa.a: Ritu probably felt belittled and hurt, and her own fear of debt was brushed aside.

grounding: An advisor's note shows co-founders whose argument about direction turns personal, who notice contempt as the sign to stop, separate idea from person and set decision rules with outside help.

Thursday, 10 p.m.

Today I said something I'm ashamed of. Sangeeta wants to take the bank loan and move our tiffin service into a proper kitchen. I think we're not ready. We've argued about it for weeks. Today, when she said, "You never want to grow," I said, "Maybe because I'm the only one who reads the numbers." And I rolled my eyes. She walked out.

On the bus home I saw it. We've stopped arguing about the loan. We're arguing about each other. That eye-roll was contempt, and I don't want to be that person with her.

I called her at eight. "Sorry. That was mean, and not true." She said, "I was unfair too."

We agreed on two things:
1. The idea is on the table, not the person.
2. We'll ask Farida ma'am from the women's business network to help us decide.

Meeting her Monday. I still think we're not ready. But I'm Kalyani, her partner, not her enemy.

qa.q: Where does Sangeeta want to move the tiffin service?
qa.a: She wants to move it into a proper kitchen.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel on the bus home?
qa.a: Kalyani felt ashamed, seeing that the eye-roll showed contempt.

qa.q: What did Kalyani and Sangeeta agree, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To keep the idea separate from the person and to ask an outside advisor to help them decide, so the disagreement doesn't damage the partnership.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta have felt when Kalyani rolled her eyes?
qa.a: Sangeeta likely felt belittled and angry, which is why she walked out.

In Maheshwar, Charu and Afreen ran a small handloom unit with six looms in an old house by the ghats. The year the orders stopped, Charu's own family begged her to shut it. Afreen stayed. She sold her gold earrings to pay the weavers for two months and never once mentioned it.

Now, three years later, a Delhi boutique had ordered two hundred saris. Charu stood in the courtyard watching the weavers and felt her throat tighten with gratitude.

She didn't want it to stay a feeling. That evening she brought a signboard painter. The old sign said "Charu Handlooms". The new one said "Charu and Afreen Handlooms".

Afreen came out with chai and stopped. "What is this?"

"What it always should have been. And from next month, we look at the accounts together every Sunday. You'll never have to guess how we're doing."

Afreen didn't say anything. She just put the chai down and hugged her.

passage:
Monday night.

Another client call I ran alone. Another invoice Pooja sent in her name. We started this design studio as equals, fifty-fifty. Now I do all the client work and the late nights, and Pooja "handles strategy", which as far as I can tell means lunch meetings and our shared social media page.

I counted this month: I billed 140 hours. She billed 30. We took home the same.

I feel used. And scared, because this studio is my whole life, and if I push, it might fall apart.

But I'm Ganga, and I didn't leave my old job to become someone's unpaid assistant.

So tomorrow I'll say it plainly: "The work split is 80-20 and the pay is 50-50. That isn't fair." I've written a one-page proposal: pay linked to hours, both our names on client work. If she won't discuss it by the end of the month, I'll talk to a lawyer about leaving.

My hands are shaking writing that. But it's written.

qa.q: How many hours did Ganga bill this month?
qa.a: Ganga billed 140 hours.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling as she wrote this entry?
qa.a: Ganga felt used and scared, afraid that pushing back might make the studio fall apart.

qa.q: What is Ganga's plan, and why is it a strong one?
qa.a: To name the imbalance plainly, propose a written fix, and be ready to leave with a lawyer's help if nothing changes, so Ganga isn't stuck being taken advantage of.

qa.q: How might Pooja see the studio's work split?
qa.a: Pooja may believe her strategy work is equally valuable and not notice how uneven the hours have become.

grounding: A diary entry shows someone whose business partner makes them carry more work for the same pay, who states the imbalance, proposes a written fix and prepares to walk away.

The co-working space in Koramangala had been theirs for three years. On the last day, Suraj sat alone in the empty cabin while the movers took the whiteboard with Chinmay's handwriting still on it: "Year 5: 1 million farmers."

The split had been bitter. Chinmay had wanted to sell; Suraj hadn't. Now the lawyers were handling the shares, and Suraj was angry. But under the anger was something he hadn't expected. He missed it. The late-night biryani. The whiteboard. The dream.

The community manager, Leena, knocked. "You okay?"

"Grieving a company," he said, and laughed shakily. "Is that stupid?"

"No. People cry here every month."

That evening Chinmay called about the share transfer. Suraj said, "Let's keep that with the lawyers. I'm not ready to talk about money and feelings in the same call." Chinmay agreed.

Suraj took a photo of the whiteboard before it went. He'd look at it someday and learn from it.

qa.a: It said "Year 5: 1 million farmers."

qa.q: What did Suraj feel beneath his anger on the last day?
qa.a: Suraj felt grief, missing the partnership, the late nights and the shared dream.

qa.a: Keeping money talks with the lawyers and away from raw feelings lets him mourn honestly without making the separation worse.

passage:
Rafiq,

The lawyers finished the paperwork yesterday. The company is closed. I didn't expect to feel this way.

I thought I'd feel angry, and I did, for months. About the investor you brought in, about the fights. But this morning I passed the café where we sketched the first app on a napkin, and I had to sit on the steps outside. It felt like mourning.

I'm not writing to reopen any of the settlement. That part is done and it should stay with the lawyers. I'm writing because I don't want five years to end with only emails from our advocates.

We built something good, and we both learned a lot about what we'd do differently. I know I'll choose a partner more carefully next time, and I'll write things down from day one.

I hope you're doing well. I mean that.

Karthik

At the agency, the glass meeting room was empty except for Madhav and Devika. Her laptop was closed. Her jaw was tight.

Madhav knew why. Last week, he had pitched the hotel campaign to the client alone, and when the client praised it, he hadn't mentioned that half the ideas were Devika's. The client had emailed the team thanking "Madhav's vision".

He had spent the weekend composing defences. She'd taken credit for the logo in March. She'd skipped the Monday call. He threw them all away.

"Devika. I took credit for your ideas in the pitch. That was wrong, and I knew it while I was doing it. I've already emailed the client to say the concept was ours together, and I've copied you. I'd like you to lead the next presentation."

Devika looked at him. "I'm still angry."

"I know. You don't have to forgive me today. I'm just telling you I own it."

qa.a: It thanked "Madhav's vision".

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling as he threw away his defences?
qa.a: Madhav felt guilty and ashamed, knowing he had wronged Devika and that excuses would only prolong the hurt.

qa.q: How did Madhav try to make things right?

passage:
Sachin,

You asked me on Friday why I did it. I didn't have a good answer then. Here's an honest one.

When our catering business was slow last year, I used our shared client list to get orders for my own side business. Eleven clients. I told myself you'd done something similar with the Dubai contact. That was an excuse, and I knew it. What I did was worse, and you found out from a client, not from me.

I'm sorry. I know that word doesn't fix much.

Here's what I'm offering: I've closed the side business. I'll transfer the profit from those eleven orders into the company account this week; our accountant has the figures. And if you want me to step back from client work for a while, I'll accept that.

I'm not asking you to forgive me. I'm asking you to let me show, over time, that I've changed.

Vijay

qa.q: How many clients did Vijay take from the shared list?
qa.a: Vijay took eleven clients.

qa.q: How does Vijay feel while writing this letter?
qa.a: Vijay feels guilty and ashamed, admitting there was no good answer and that the excuse didn't hold.

qa.q: Why is Vijay right to drop the Dubai excuse?
qa.a: Self-justifying with what Sachin did would keep the injury alive; owning it fully and offering real restitution gives repair a chance.

qa.q: How might Sachin have felt finding out from a client?
qa.a: Sachin likely felt betrayed and humiliated, learning about it from an outsider instead of from Vijay.

grounding: A letter shows someone who realises they wronged a business partner who is now hurt, who owns it clearly, offers restitution and accepts consequences without demanding forgiveness.

passage:
At the cooperative bank branch in Sangamner, the staff had known Noor as the clerk at counter three for four years. On Monday she walked in as branch supervisor.

She felt it at once. Usha, who had been there eleven years, said "Good morning, madam" with a small smile that wasn't friendly. The peon hurried to bring Noor tea first. Nobody asked her anything.

Noor's stomach was tight all morning. They think I'm too young. They think I got it because I passed an exam.

At lunch she didn't give a speech. She sat with the staff at their usual table and said, "I don't know the loan approvals side the way Usha tai does. I'll need to learn from her. And please call me Noor, not madam."

Usha looked surprised. "The farm loans are tricky. I'll show you tomorrow."

At the end of the month, the branch cleared its loan backlog for the first time in a year. Usha stayed back to help Noor with the report.

qa.q: How many years had Usha been at the branch?
qa.a: Usha had been there eleven years.

qa.q: What was Noor worried about on her first morning as supervisor?
qa.a: Noor felt insecure and anxious, her stomach tight, fearing the staff thought she was too young to deserve it.

qa.q: What did Noor do instead of acting bossy?
qa.a: She admitted what she didn't know, asked to learn from Usha, dropped the "madam", and let the results build her authority.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Noor asked to learn from her?
qa.a: Usha was surprised and probably felt respected, which softened her and led her to offer help.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman newly promoted over former peers who fears they think she doesn't deserve it, who is honest about what she doesn't know and lets results build authority.
